Blind Bar 01 · supplement teardown

Three carousels, unlabeled. Same brief, same brand pool, $0 in images, built by two different paths. Read each as a LinkedIn swipe, then answer the one falsifiable question at the bottom. The key that maps 1/2/3 to the paths sits in a sidecar file; open it after you have tapped.

1

caption
410 AG1 ads were live on Meta when I opened the Ad Library this morning.

I read forty of them. One scoop. Seventy-five-plus ingredients. Foundational nutrition. A creator says the decade line in her kitchen. Hugh Jackman calls it a no-brainer. A $72 welcome kit waits at the bottom of every one of them.

Four hundred and ten costumes. Three sentences.

That is what creative fatigue looks like from the inside, and it is almost never a creative problem. The team keeps ordering formats because nobody chose the argument. A hook changes the doorway. An angle changes the argument.

AG1 has three it could lead with. The ingredient count, which Huel answers with 91 and Ka'Chava with 85, so it stopped being an argument years ago. The outcome, what a person actually feels by week three, which is honest and specific and almost never in the ads. And the ritual, the same glass on the same counter, still there in March.

That last one matters more than it used to. On 3 February 2026 a class action, Hoke v. AG1, was filed over subscriptions people say they did not choose. Strip the legal language and it is a buyer sentence: I did not decide to still be paying for this. Four hundred and ten ads, and not one of them argues for month three.

Choose the argument before you multiply it. Three campaign angles, one lead recommendation, before the next creative round. DM ANGLE.

2

caption
Open the ad library of any greens powder and read ten ads. One scoop. A number of ingredients: 75, 85, 91, depending on the bag. Daily, foundational, complete. A creator in a kitchen, a welcome kit, a subscription pre-selected at checkout.

Different costumes, one sentence. The whole aisle is running the same argument with a different count in the headline.

When everyone owns a claim, nobody does. So the teams do what teams do when the numbers soften: more UGC, more statics, another creator, another round. They call it creative fatigue. It is an unmade decision.

A greens powder can argue three things. The count, which is the category's wallpaper now. The outcome, what a person feels by week three, which is honest and specific and rarely in the ads. Or the ritual, the same glass on the same counter in March, which is the only argument that answers the question every subscription-first funnel begs: will I still want this next month.

Choose the argument before you multiply it. DM ANGLE.

3

caption
You can see creative fatigue from the outside. Open AG1's page in the Meta Ad Library: about 410 ads live this morning, a $72 welcome kit, a Hugh Jackman headline, a creator saying the decade line in a new kitchen. It looks like a production problem. It reads like one in the Monday meeting too, which is why the fix is always more: more UGC, more statics, another creator, another round.

The diagnosis is wrong. The campaign underneath has no chosen argument. A hook changes the doorway. An angle changes the argument, and the argument has not moved since the first bag shipped.

Two groups are already arguing AG1's month three, and neither is AG1. IM8 runs a public switch page: no vitamin D in the scoop, refrigerate after opening. A plaintiff filed Hoke v. AG1 on 3 February 2026 over subscriptions people say they did not choose. Under both sits one buyer question: will I still drink this in March.

Lead with March. The ritual angle. One scoop, the same glass, still on the counter in month three. It is honest, it is specific, and it answers the challenger and the plaintiff in the same sentence.

Choose the product truth, the buyer tension, and the proof boundary before the next brief. Then build. DM ANGLE.
